strengths: The core idea of using semi-supervised learning with self-consistency losses to improve the robustness of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) on out-of-distribution (unlabeled) data is novel and elegant.
The paper provides solid theoretical support, proving that the self-consistency loss on unlabeled data is strictly proper (Propositions 1-4).
The writing is exceptionally clear, and the explanation of the self-consistency ratio and its relation to marginal likelihood is easy to follow.

Initial toy experiments on the multivariate Gaussian model demonstrate a significant reduction in posterior bias and MMD compared to standard NPE, even when only a handful of unlabeled target observations are provided.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is extremely limited, as the method is only tested on a single toy problem (a conjugate multivariate Gaussian model). There are no tests on standard simulation-based inference (SBI) benchmarks (such as sbi-benchmark, including tasks like Two Moons, Lotka-Volterra, or SIR), which typically feature complex geometries, multi-modality, or intractable likelihoods.

The paper explicitly self-identifies as a 'work in progress' and a 'proof-of-concept paper' (with a prominent disclaimer box on the first page noting that further experiments are planned for the full version). While the transparency is appreciated, submitting an incomplete manuscript with missing core experiments does not meet the standards of a top-tier AI conference.

When the likelihood $p(x|\theta)$ is intractable (the standard setting for SBI/ABI), the method requires training a neural surrogate likelihood estimator. As shown in Figure 3 (top row), when using an estimated likelihood, the performance of the posterior estimator degrades considerably, particularly for the posterior standard deviation bias. This limitation restricts the practical applicability of the method in realistic SBI scenarios.

The variance estimation in Eq. (4) relies on sampling from a proposal distribution $p_C(\theta)$. The paper lacks a detailed discussion or empirical study on the behavior and stability of this Monte Carlo approximation in high-dimensional parameter spaces (e.g., $D=100$), where finding overlapping regions of density is notoriously challenging.

strengths: The core idea of leveraging Bayesian self-consistency as an unsupervised loss on unlabeled out-of-distribution (OOD) data is elegant, intuitive, and highly promising for addressing the robustness issues of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI).
The theoretical properties are well-formalized, demonstrating the strict properness of the proposed semi-supervised loss.
The writing is exceptionally clear, and the paper is very well-structured and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The paper is explicitly self-identified as a 'work in progress' and a 'proof-of-concept paper'. A prominent box on the first page acknowledges that key experiments on common benchmarks, challenging posterior geometries (e.g., multi-modality, funnels), and very high-dimensional scenarios are missing and deferred to a 'full version'.

The evaluation is extremely limited, relying solely on a simple, conjugate multivariate Gaussian model ('normal means problem'). Standard simulation-based inference (SBI) benchmark models (such as Two Moons, SLCP, Lotka-Volterra, or SIR) are completely absent.

The method shows a notable drop in performance when the likelihood is estimated rather than known (Figure 3, top row). Since SBI typically deals with implicit likelihoods (where the likelihood is unknown), this represents a major practical limitation that is not sufficiently addressed.

The methodological novelty over existing work (specifically Schmitt et al., 2024 [34]) is limited, as the core self-consistency loss formulation is directly adapted, and the primary contribution lies in applying it to a semi-supervised setup.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly critical and open challenge in amortized Bayesian inference (ABI): the lack of robustness and susceptibility to severe bias/variance collapse when applied to out-of-distribution (OOD) or misspecified data.

The formulation of a semi-supervised approach using self-consistency losses on unlabeled data is a very promising direction, as it allows utilizing unlabelled real-world observations directly during training.
The paper is well-written, clear, and provides solid theoretical justification (Propositions 1-4) showing that the proposed semi-supervised objective is strictly proper.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is extremely limited. The authors only evaluate the proposed method on a toy multivariate Gaussian model (normal means problem). There are no standard simulation-based inference (SBI) benchmarks (such as Lotka-Volterra, SIR, Two Moons, or Jansy) or real-world scientific simulators.

As the authors explicitly state in the box on Page 1, 'This paper is still work in progress.' While the proof-of-concept is interesting, a complete submission to a top-tier AI venue requires comprehensive evaluation beyond toy Gaussian models.

In many practical SBI settings, the likelihood is intractable (likelihood-free inference). When the likelihood has to be estimated (as shown in Figure 3, top row), the performance of the self-consistency loss degrades significantly, introducing visible bias in the posterior standard deviation. This indicates that the method's practical utility might be limited when joint posterior-likelihood estimation is required, which needs to be explored on more complex models.

The methodological novelty over Schmitt et al. (2024) [34] is somewhat limited, as the core self-consistency loss and its variance-based formulation are directly taken from prior work. The primary contribution here is the application of this loss to unlabeled OOD data.

strengths: Novel and Elegant Idea: The application of Bayesian self-consistency as a semi-supervised loss on unlabeled, out-of-simulation or real-world data is highly innovative. It elegantly circumvents the lack of ground-truth parameter 'labels' for real-world observations.
Theoretical Grounding: The authors provide solid theoretical justification by proving the strict properness of the proposed self-consistency losses under different conditions (Propositions 1-4).

Excellent Robustness Improvements: The empirical results demonstrate remarkable improvements in posterior accuracy on out-of-distribution test data where standard NPE collapses or becomes highly biased.

Thorough Empirical Analysis: The synthetic multivariate normal case study systematically explores various factors (dimensionality up to 100, number of unlabeled samples, summary networks, and estimated likelihoods). The real-world air traffic forecasting model further validates the utility of the method on real datasets compared to Stan (MCMC).
Clarity of Writing: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with clear mathematical formulations, illustrative figures, and a detailed appendix.
weaknesses: Reliance on Likelihood Tractability: The method relies on evaluating the likelihood $p(x|\theta)$. In many classic simulation-based inference (SBI) settings, the likelihood is intractable. While the authors show that the method can work with a trained surrogate likelihood $q(x|\theta)$, the performance degrades compared to the known likelihood case, and learning a surrogate on a misspecified simulator remains a bottleneck.

Lack of Empirical Comparison to Other Robustness Methods: The evaluation compares standard NPE against the proposed NPE+SC, but does not benchmark against other existing methods designed to handle simulator misspecification or domain shift (e.g., post-hoc corrections or calibration-based approaches). Comparing against at least one such baseline would strengthen the paper's claims.

Computational Cost of Estimating the Loss: Minimizing the variance of the log self-consistency ratio requires sampling $L$ parameters from a proposal distribution per training iteration. The paper does not thoroughly discuss how training complexity and the choice of $L$ scale with the parameter dimensionality $D$.

strengths: The paper introduces an elegant, mathematically sound, and novel semi-supervised learning framework for amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) by leveraging Bayesian self-consistency.
The proposed method addresses a critical bottleneck in ABI, which is the lack of robustness and high bias when performing inference on out-of-distribution or model-misspecified observations.
The theoretical foundation is solid, including proofs showing that the self-consistency loss is a strictly proper scoring rule.

The empirical evaluation is convincing: the toy multivariate normal model explores various dimensions, while the real-world European air passenger traffic case study shows that the method successfully aligns with gold-standard MCMC (Stan) where standard NPE completely fails.
weaknesses: The method requires evaluation of the likelihood $p(x|\theta)$. While the authors demonstrate that an estimated surrogate likelihood $q(x|\theta)$ can be used, the performance degrades compared to the known likelihood case. Given that intractable likelihoods are the primary motivation for simulation-based inference, this limitation and its practical implications deserve more thorough discussion.

Evaluating the self-consistency loss requires sampling $L$ parameters from a proposal distribution and conducting multiple density evaluations under both the posterior and likelihood estimators for each of the $M$ unlabeled points. This could significantly increase the computational cost per training step, but a detailed analysis of the training time complexity and trade-offs is missing.
The experiments lack comparison with other existing robust or adaptive ABI methods (e.g., post-hoc corrections or adversarial defense methods), comparing primarily against standard NPE and MCMC.

strengths: Addresses a critical and highly relevant problem in Amortized Bayesian Inference (ABI): robustness to out-of-distribution data and model misspecification.
The semi-supervised framework using Bayesian self-consistency is mathematically elegant and well-founded.
Clear mathematical proofs showing that the joint semi-supervised objective is strictly proper.
Strong empirical performance on the tasks evaluated, showing that the proposed self-consistency loss prevents the posterior collapse typically observed in standard NPE.
weaknesses: Limited Baseline Comparison: The paper fails to compare the proposed method with other established robust or adaptive SBI approaches, such as post-hoc corrections (Ward et al., 2022), neural calibration methods (Wehenkel et al., 2024), or other domain-adaptation methods in SBI. Simply comparing to standard NPE (which is known to fail out-of-distribution) is insufficient to show the superiority of the method.

Limited Novelty: The formulation of the Bayesian self-consistency loss is heavily inherited from Schmitt et al. (2024) [38]. The transition to applying it on unlabeled data (semi-supervised) is highly logical, but the underlying theoretical machinery and loss formulation are largely incremental.

Strong Dependency on Tractable Likelihoods: A key benefit of SBI is handling intractable likelihoods. The self-consistency loss requires calculating $p(x|\theta)$. While the authors propose learning a surrogate likelihood $q(x|\theta)$ jointly, the results in Figure 4 show a noticeable degradation in performance (with larger standard deviation bias and MMD) when the likelihood is estimated rather than analytical.

Simplicity of Empirical Tasks: The evaluation tasks are limited to a multivariate Gaussian and an AR(1) process. While useful as controlled testbeds, they are computationally simple and have analytical or easily tractable likelihoods. Evaluation on standard, complex, and high-dimensional SBI benchmarks (e.g., Hodgkin-Huxley model, epidemiological models) is missing.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly critical and open problem in amortized Bayesian inference (ABI): the lack of robustness when applied to out-of-simulation (OOD) or misspecified data.
The proposed semi-supervised approach leverages Bayesian self-consistency to train on unlabeled data, providing a elegant formulation that does not require ground-truth parameters.

The authors provide strong theoretical guarantees showing that the self-consistency loss is strictly proper, indicating that there is no trade-off between standard simulation-based objectives and the proposed self-consistency objective.

Comprehensive empirical evaluations are performed across a diverse range of tasks, including a controllable multivariate normal model, real-world air passenger traffic forecasting, the Hodgkin-Huxley model of neuron activation, and high-dimensional MNIST image denoising.
The paper is very well-written, clearly structured, and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The proposed method relies on having access to either the analytic likelihood $p(x|\theta)$ or a trained neural likelihood surrogate $q(x|\theta)$. This requirement limits its applicability to pure simulation-based inference (SBI) settings where the likelihood is completely intractable.
When a neural likelihood surrogate is used instead of the analytic likelihood, the empirical performance slightly degrades, as shown in the bias of the posterior standard deviation in Figure 7.

The choice and design of the proposal distribution $p_C(\theta)$ over the parameter space can significantly influence the training dynamics and gradients. While the authors outline various options, a more detailed empirical analysis of how different choices of $p_C(\theta)$ affect performance would strengthen the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and well-known limitation of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI)—its vulnerability to domain shifts and simulation gaps—by introducing an elegant semi-supervised approach.
The theoretical foundation is solid, proving the strict properness of the proposed semi-supervised loss function (combining standard simulation losses with self-consistency losses).

The evaluation is exceptionally thorough, spanning a controllable multivariate normal benchmark, a real-world macroeconomic forecasting model (air passenger traffic), a complex biophysical system (Hodgkin-Huxley), and high-dimensional image denoising (MNIST).

The results demonstrate remarkable improvements in robustness and out-of-distribution generalization, with posterior estimates aligning closely with gold-standard MCMC/Stan benchmarks while retaining fast amortized inference.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, clearly structured, and provides comprehensive details and hyperparameters in the appendix to facilitate reproducibility.
weaknesses: The self-consistency loss relies on fast, tractable density evaluations of the likelihood. When the likelihood must be estimated using a neural surrogate (as in NPLE), joint training becomes necessary, which can introduce additional bias and variance in the estimated posteriors.

The choice of the proposal distribution $p_C(\theta)$ used to compute the variance in the self-consistency loss is highly critical for training stability and dynamics, but the paper offers limited general guidelines on how to select or adapt it during training.

The reliance on density evaluations limits applicability to modern free-form generative architectures, such as flow matching or score-based diffusion, which do not offer cheap exact likelihood evaluations without costly numerical integration.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated focus on addressing a critical bottleneck of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI): the lack of robustness to out-of-distribution (OOD) data or model misspecification.
Methodological novelty in framing Bayesian self-consistency as a semi-supervised loss that leverages unlabeled real-world data without requiring ground-truth parameters.
Solid theoretical foundation, specifically providing proofs of strict properness for the semi-supervised self-consistency loss formulations.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse tasks including a toy Gaussian model, a real-world econometric forecasting model, the high-dimensional Hodgkin-Huxley model, and image denoising on MNIST.
weaknesses: The method requires evaluating the likelihood function $p(x^*|\theta)$. In many simulation-based inference (SBI) scenarios, the likelihood is completely intractable. While the authors propose estimating the likelihood jointly (NPLE), neural likelihood estimators can also fail spectacularly on out-of-distribution observations $x^*$. The potential compounding of errors when using an approximate likelihood on OOD data is not thoroughly discussed or quantified.

There is a lack of empirical comparisons against other robust amortized inference baselines. Comparing solely against standard NPE/NPLE is a start, but comparing with alternative robustification strategies (e.g., post-hoc correction methods, calibration-set-based methods, or generalized Bayesian inference) would strengthen the evaluation.

The choice of the proposal distribution $p_C(\theta)$ is crucial for the variance-based self-consistency loss. The paper notes that its empirical consequences are difficult to anticipate, but provides limited guidelines or sensitivity analyses on how this choice affects convergence and final performance.

strengths: The proposed semi-supervised framework is mathematically elegant and theoretically sound. The authors prove that the self-consistency loss is strictly proper, meaning it targets the true analytical posterior and does not introduce undesirable regularization trade-offs.
It addresses a highly critical and practical limitation of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI), which is the failure to generalize to out-of-simulation/out-of-distribution real observations.

The empirical evaluation is exceptionally thorough and covers diverse domains: a controllable toy multivariate normal model, real-world autoregressive air passenger forecasting, a highly non-linear differential equation model in neuroscience (Hodgkin-Huxley), and high-dimensional image denoising (MNIST).
The paper is exceptionally well-written, clear, and easy to follow. The appendices contain comprehensive details, proofs, and exhaustive experimental results.
weaknesses: The method requires evaluating the likelihood function $p(x|\theta)$ (or a surrogate $q(x|\theta)$). In many simulation-based inference (SBI) scenarios, the likelihood is completely intractable. Although the paper shows that the method works with an estimated likelihood, the performance in this setting shows higher bias and is less robust than with a known likelihood.

Evaluating the self-consistency loss during training requires sampling parameters $\theta^{(l)} \sim q_t(\theta|x^*)$ and performing density/likelihood evaluations at each training step. This inevitably increases training time, but a quantitative analysis of this computational overhead compared to standard NPE is missing.

Using the current approximate posterior $q_t(\theta|x^*)$ as the proposal distribution $p_C(\theta)$ can lead to training instabilities (such as exploding gradients) early in training when the posterior is poorly estimated. Although the authors mitigate this using a linear schedule for the coupling weight $\lambda$, a more thorough sensitivity analysis of this scheduling would be helpful.

strengths: Strong Motivation and Novelty: The idea of using Bayesian self-consistency as a semi-supervised objective on unlabeled (possibly real-world) data is highly elegant and novel. It provides a principled, theoretically sound framework to tackle the out-of-distribution and model-misspecification problems in amortized Bayesian inference without needing ground-truth parameters.

Solid Theoretical Foundation: The paper provides clear proofs of the strict properness of the proposed losses under known likelihood (Propositions 1-3) and extends the concept to likelihood estimators (Proposition 4).

Diverse and Challenging Evaluations: The authors evaluate their method on a wide variety of tasks—ranging from an analytical multivariate normal model to real-world autoregressive modeling of air traffic, a highly non-linear biological Hodgkin-Huxley model, and high-dimensional MNIST image denoising.

Strong Empirical Performance: The proposed NPE + SC method consistently and significantly outperforms standard NPE and state-of-the-art robustness/domain adaptation methods (like NPE-DANN, NPE-MMD, and NNPE) in the out-of-distribution regime, aligning closely with gold-standard MCMC (Stan) baselines.

Clarity and Quality of Presentation: The paper is very well-written, with high-quality figures and an easy-to-follow structure. The detailed explanations in the appendix (including the FAQ section) are extremely helpful for understanding the method's practical implementation and intuition.
weaknesses: Dependence on Likelihood Evaluability: The self-consistency loss relies on the ability to evaluate the likelihood $p(x^*|\theta)$. When the likelihood is completely intractable and must be estimated via a neural surrogate (as shown in Figure 7, top row), the performance (e.g., standard deviation bias) deteriorates compared to the known likelihood case. This is a common bottleneck in simulation-based inference (SBI) that limits the general applicability of the method to fully likelihood-free settings.

Computational Overhead during Training: Evaluating the self-consistency loss requires drawing multiple parameter samples $\theta \sim q(\theta|x^*)$ (e.g., $L=32$ in the experiments) and computing both likelihood and posterior densities for each. This introduces a non-trivial computational overhead during the training phase, which should be discussed or quantified more explicitly in the main text.

strengths: Elegant Methodological Framework: The paper extends the concept of self-consistency losses to a semi-supervised setup, utilizing unlabeled real data to guide the neural posterior estimator in out-of-simulation regions. This is a very natural and effective way to address the robustness issue in amortized Bayesian inference.

Strong Theoretical Foundation: The authors prove that the self-consistency losses are strictly proper and directly target the true posterior without altering the underlying statistical model (unlike standard regularizers or UDA methods that shift the target).

Convincing and Diverse Evaluation: The empirical evaluation spans synthetic Gaussian models, real-world autoregressive traffic forecasting (compared to MCMC via Stan), a 7-parameter biological mechanistic model (Hodgkin-Huxley), and high-dimensional image denoising (MNIST). The performance gains over standard NPE/NPLE and alternative robustness methods (like NPE-DANN, NPE-MMD, and NNPE) are highly convincing.
Amortization Maintained: Unlike post-hoc correction methods (e.g., using MCMC at test-time), this approach preserves the fast inference speed of amortized networks.

Clarity and Quality of Writing: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with highly illustrative figures (e.g., Figure 1 and the MNIST denoising maps) and a detailed appendix containing comprehensive setup details and proofs.
weaknesses: Performance in Likelihood-Free Settings: The self-consistency loss fundamentally relies on evaluating the joint density p(x, θ) = p(x|θ)p(θ). When the likelihood p(x|θ) is intractable (which is common in simulation-based inference), one must train a surrogate neural likelihood estimator. As shown in the top row of Figure 7, estimating the likelihood leads to noticeably higher bias in the posterior standard deviation compared to having the analytic likelihood. This dependency on surrogate accuracy is a key limitation that deserves more prominent discussion.

Computational Overhead during Training: Calculating the self-consistency loss requires generating samples from the posterior network q_t(θ|x*) and evaluating the likelihood at every training iteration. A direct comparison of the training time/overhead (e.g., epoch duration) with and without the SC loss would help practitioners weigh the cost against the robustness benefits.

Sensitivity to Hyperparameters: In high-dimensional settings, the self-consistency loss can be unstable at initialization, requiring a linear scheduling of λ. More analysis or empirical results demonstrating the sensitivity of the method to different choices of λ schedules would make the method easier to deploy.
